title: Neural Polaron: Learning Quasiparticle Operators in Quantum Many-Body Systems
abstract: Understanding dynamical properties of quantum many-body systems remains a central challenge because excitations generally require information beyond a ground-state wave function. Here we introduce a neural polaron ansatz that represents quasiparticle excitations by neural many-body operators acting on a correlated ground state. Instead of learning an independent excited-state wave function, the method parameterizes a local dressing operator through a compact neural head defined on the feature map of a pretrained ground-state network. This operator-based construction builds in translation symmetry, momentum resolution, and quasiparticle locality, while separating ground-state correlations from excitation-specific dressing. We benchmark the method on the square-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model, where it accurately reproduces magnon dispersions and spectral weights over a broad range of frustration. In particular, it captures nontrivial many-body features including the $(π,0)$ anomaly and its progressive softening with increasing $J_2/J_1$. These results establish neural operators as a physically transparent route for extending neural quantum states from ground-state properties to dynamical response.
summary: The paper introduces the 'neural polaron' ansatz to calculate quantum excitations by modeling quasiparticle operators as local dressings on top of a learned ground state. By applying this method to the $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model, the authors successfully reproduce complex dynamical features like magnon dispersions and roton minima. This establishes neural networks as a powerful tool for extending quantum state descriptions from static properties to full dynamic response.
main_problem: The central challenge is understanding the dynamical properties (excitation spectra) of quantum many-body systems, which require information beyond a simple ground-state wave function.
main_result: The proposed neural polaron ansatz accurately reproduces magnon dispersions and spectral weights for the $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model, capturing subtle features like the $(\pi,0)$ anomaly.
method: The method parameterizes quasiparticle excitations using a local dressing operator (the 'polaron head') acting on the feature map of a pre-trained ground-state neural network, separating ground-state correlations from excitation dynamics.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the square-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model, analyzed in its Néel phase regime ($0 < J_2/J_1 < 0.4$). The Hamiltonian involves nearest-neighbor ($J_1$) and next-nearest-neighbor ($J_2$) couplings.
key_observables: Dynamical structure factor $S_{+-}(q, \omega)$, magnon dispersions, spectral weights, and the quasiparticle residue $	ilde{Z}_q$.
important_parameters: $J_1$, $J_2$, and the ratio $J_2/J_1$; momentum vectors like $q = (\pi, 0)$ and $q = (\pi/2, \pi/2)$.
main_assumptions: The excitation operator is assumed to be local or quasi-local; the ground state is parameterized by a CNN structure, and the ansatz relies on an inductive bias separating dressing from correlations.
figures_summary: Figures compare $S_{+-}(q, \omega)$ across varying frustration ($J_2/J_1$), showing agreement with benchmarks. Other figures illustrate energy convergence based on the spatial extent of the neural head architecture.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the ansatz by separating ground-state encoding from excitation dressing. It then validates this structure by testing its ability to reproduce known physical results (magnon dispersions) across varying lattice parameters, concluding with an analysis of the required complexity of the local operator.
why_interesting: This work provides a physically transparent and computationally scalable framework for calculating dynamic response functions in strongly correlated systems, bridging the gap between static ground-state neural representations and time/momentum-dependent physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the neural polaron ansatz. A ground- state neural network maps a spin configuration σ to a spa- tial feature map h(r; σ) that encodes many-body correlations. The same feature map is used to construct both the ground- state amplitude Ψ0(σ) via a global readout and quasiparticle excitations via a local neural head function fθ. The head acts on a finite spatial neighborhood of each site, defining a local excitation operator Or ≡fθ h h Pr

FIG. 2. Exact diagonalization benchmark on a 4 × 4 lattice. Shown is the dynamical structure factor S+−(q, ω) at fixed momentum q = (π, 0) for J2/J1 = 0, 0.2, and 0.4. The neu- ral polaron results (dashed lines) are compared with exact diagonalization (solid lines). Both the excitation energy and the spectral weight of the quasiparticle peak are accurately reproduced across the interaction range, demonstrating that the ansatz captures the position and residue of the magnon pole.

FIG. 3. Expressibility of the neural polaron head function on an 8 × 8 lattice at q = (π, 0) and J2/J1 = 0. (a) Energy versus training epoch for different head architectures charac- terized by kernel size and depth. Curves show seed-averaged results, with shaded regions indicating seed-to-seed variation. Increasing the spatial extent of the head systematically lowers the variational energy, indicating that a finite spatial dress- ing cloud is required for an accurate description of the (π, 0) quasiparticle. (b) Estimated energy Eest as a function of head architecture (size, depth).

FIG. 4. Momentum-resolved dynamical structure factor S+−(q, ω) on an 8 × 8 lattice along the high-symmetry path (π/2, π/2) →(π, 0) →(π, π) →(π/2, π/2) for representa- tive values of J2/J1. Color maps show the neural polaron results. For (a) J2/J1 = 0, quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) data [41] is overlaid for comparison. The ansatz accurately reproduces the magnon dispersion and spectral weight, in- cluding the roton-like minimum near q = (π, 0). As J2/J1 increases (see panel (b), (c)), the evolution of dispersion and intensity reflects the enhanced frustration and modification of quasiparticle dressing.
